newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria turns up heat in Creditanstalt sale saga.
newsitem.headline: Austria turns up heat in Creditanstalt sale saga.

text.p: Austria's government on Tuesday turned up the heat on an Austro-Italian consortium bidding for privatisation candidate Creditanstalt, saying their time was up unless the group came up with a final offer by Friday.
"We want an offer, a price and a date," Finance Minister Viktor Klima told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
If the consortium around savings bank Die Erste and insurer EA-Generali failed to comply, "we will begin a new search for potential buyers", he added.

The original deadline expired last Friday, but Klima on Monday said he had agreed to give the group, the only known bidder for the government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt-Bankverein, a last chance.

Die Erste Oesterreichische Spar-Casse Bank wants to set up a holding with Creditanstalt, but its partners have voiced increasing concern about the strong position Die Erste -- barely a third the size of Creditanstalt -- would have in the proposed holding structure.
Apart from EA-Generali, majority-owned by Italy's Assicurazioni Generali, the consortium includes German heavyweight Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana SpA.

The latest twist in the six-year long privatisation saga of Austria's number two bank appeared to have deepened the rift between the partners. Die Erste last week indicated the talks had hit a snag, while Commerzbank was reported to be considering leaving the group altogether.

Viktor Klima, a member of the ruling Social Democrats, meanwhile appeared to be considering the possibility of a new bidder entering the race. "In principle we aim to sell the entire 70 percent stake. But there are alternatives," he said.
"My advisors (investment house JP Morgan) and I have received several calls from interested parties. But there is no final offer yet," he added without elaborating further.
Senior executives at Creditanstalt desperately appealed for a speedy conclusion to the seemingly endless privatisation project, which they say is damaging the bank's image abroad.

"Such complex negotiations often look more murky than they actually are," supervisory board president Walter Fremuth told Austrian news agency APA. "I am confident we will have a speedy solution. This discussion is not good for Creditanstalt."
The debate about Austria's number two bank, founded in 1863 by the Rothschilds and one-time banker to the Habsburg empire, has been politically charged since it began six years ago.

The conservative People's Party (OeVP), the Social Democrats' junior coalition partner, has repeatedly said it wants the bank to remain under domestic control and has warned not to sell out the "family silver" to foreign buyers.
But the Social Democrats have been pressing for a speedy sale to help ease the Finance Minister's growing budget woes.

Several foreign bidders, including Allianz of Germany and Switzerland's CS Holding have lost interest in Creditanstalt over the past years because of what they felt was a bias against foreigners in Austria.

Creditanstalt, with total assets of about 650 billion schillings ($62.14 billion), has become one of the most successful players on the emerging markets of central and eastern Europe. ($1=10.46 Schilling)
